messages.subject: How can one add a quantty generated in the "model" step to generated quantities ?
parts:
Dear list,

I am trying to  duplicate Carlin & Chib (1995) results on the modelization of the compressive strength of Pines radiata wood by two linear regressio. This is easy to do. It is also easy to write Stan code that fits those two models in parallel. One can also easily get the log-posterior densities for each of these models (see attached code and data).

What I am not able to do is to add those log-posteriors in the output sample. If I declare them in the "parameters" or "transformed parameters" block, Stan detects an affectation in the wrong block ; if I declare them in the model block, they are no longer visible in the "generated quantities" block, and Stan tells me that these variable do not exist.

This seems to be a more general problem : one cannot (currently) get samples of anything else than parameters or expressions using them. Such a possibility might be useful for (in example) to sample other derived quantities of data and parameters (yes, I'm thinking *also* about DIC/WAIC... More on this in a further post, when ready).

I see two potential solutions to this problem :
1) extend the scope of the "model"variables to the "generated quantities" block ; or
2) create a special pseudo-distribution "ident" which would be a Dirac of its argument with unit mass. This would allow to declare such quantities as paraeters, thus allowing to sample them without violating current scope rules.

Am I missing something ?

                                                                   Emmanuel Charpentier

> Dear list,

> I am trying to duplicate Carlin & Chib (1995) results on the modelization of the compressive strength of Pines radiata
> wood by two linear regressio. This is easy to do. It is also easy to write Stan code that fits those two models in
> parallel. One can also easily get the log-posterior densities for each of these models (see attached code and data).
>
> What I am not able to do is to add those log-posteriors in the output sample. If I declare them in the "parameters" or
> "transformed parameters" block, Stan detects an affectation in the wrong block ; if I declare them in the model block,
> they are no longer visible in the "generated quantities" block, and Stan tells me that these variable do not exist.

You didn't include an example, but I'm guessing you're trying
to define a transformed parameter in the model block, which is
illegal. You need to define transformed parameters in the
transformed parameter block.

> This seems to be a more general problem : one cannot (currently) get samples of anything else than parameters or
> expressions using them. Such a possibility might be useful for (in example) to sample other derived quantities of data
> and parameters (yes, I'm thinking *also* about DIC/WAIC... More on this in a further post, when ready).

Technically, the samples are just of the parameters. And the
unconstrained parameters, at that. Everything
else is derived from the parameters, including the constrained
parameters you see in the model. You can use the data to
derive quantities in either transformed parameters or generated
quantities --- the data variables are available in all subsequent
blocks.

> I see two potential solutions to this problem :
> 1) extend the scope of the "model"variables to the "generated quantities" block ; or
> 2) create a special pseudo-distribution "ident" which would be a Dirac of its argument with unit mass. This would allow
> to declare such quantities as paraeters, thus allowing to sample them without violating current scope rules.
>
> Am I missing something ?

Solution 1 could work. But if the variables have top-level
scope in the model block, you can declare them as transformed
parameters. You just have to assign them values in the
transformed parameter block. This was the way I intended this
kind of thing to be done.

Proposal 2 is both messy and difficult to implement in a general
HMC algorithm (it's possible by treating constraints the right way,
but we currently throw an error if you try to set a variable's
lower-bound and upper-bound constraint to the same value).

It's ugly in the modeling language, but it's actually more efficient
to just recompute in the generated quantities block. Any quantity that
depends on a parameter (transformed parameter, local variable in model
block) creates an automatic differentiation variable (or several), which
have to be managed dynamically in memory and are the main bottleneck
in Stan's execution speed at the moment (and in any foreseeable future
where we need to compute derivatives).

It's always a shame when implementation details intrude on an
otherwise flexible modeling language. Maybe one day we'll get more
clever in Stan program analysis and code generation so we can
optimize some of these issues away --- but we're a long way away from
thinking about this kind of thing.

- Bob

transformed parameters {
vector[2] lp;
for (i in 1:2) {
// Prior sur l'�cart-type
lp[i]<-inv_gamma_log(Sigmas[i],Alpha,Beta);
// prior sur les param�tres de r�gression
lp[i]<-lp[i]+multi_normal_log(Betas[i],Prior_mean,Prior_vcv);

This model reminds me we should check that all input characters
are ASCII. We don't explicitly support extended characters outside
the ASCII range. Presumably this just worked because you used
the Latin1 encoding, and we're not checking the high bit.

> which is somewhat counterintuitive. Furthermore, I do not think I can use the
> "Var~whatever(Pars)" notation, and I have to use the less intuitive "lp__<-lp__+wwhatever_log(Var,Pars" notation.

> Ugly.

In Stan 2, the syntax is changing to "increment_log_prob(whatever_log(Var,Pars))"

Still ugly, though.

And allowing sampling statements in the transformed parameters
block won't help with this, because it won't save the value.

The other thing to be careful about is that the ~ and <- have
slightly different interpretations. The sampling statements
drop constant terms, because we only need the log probability up
to a constant factor. The explicit _log forms do not drop any
terms.

> Yet another alternative could be to have (repeatable) "submodel" paragraphs, and a function to use their log_posterior
> in the main model. This could be worthwhile if one can factor the sampling along the same lines.

Could you write out what you think this'd look like?

We've been thinking about adding functions with and without
return types. But I'm not sure how this would help here.
Maybe something like:

log probability foo(vector[] x, vector[] y, real alpha, real beta, real<lower=0> sigma) {
for (n in 1:size(x))
y[n] ~ normal(x[n] * alpha + beta, sigma);
}

Then if you did:

lp_temp <- foo(x,y,alpha,beta,sigma);

you might get what you want.

> But one can be afraid
> of some nasty side effects, such as the effects of "cut" in BUGS (Martyn Plummer insists on the fact that a Bugs program
> using cut is no longetr the representation of a distribution ; I think he's right).

If we did this in Stan, it wouldn't behave like BUGS's cut.
It would behave like it was a macro (only with proper scope).

Martyn's right that using cut changes the interpretation of a program.
The uses I've mainly seen is to do some predictive inference using
the fitted parameters that does not feed back into model estimation.
In this case, the parameters still get the right distribution, but the
inference isn't full Bayes (though in some cases it'll give you the
same answer).

- Bob

Right-to-left (or top-to-bottom) rendering is a completely separate issue
from character encodings. The order of rendering is not part of the
Unicode standard per se, but instead a directive to something like a web
browser. Arabic's especially fun because numbers and quoted English words
go left-to-right, whereas Arabic characters go right-to-left.
> Couldn't Stan tolerate at least UTF-8 encoding of at least the comments ?

Not without a huge amount of work. C++ doesn't have the nice
built-ins that Java has for dealing with Unicode.

But part of the problem is that users are terrible at being consistent
with anything but ASCII. I've gotten mixed docs of Latin1 and UTF-8
that people have munged together in Perl or Python.

A document has to be encoding in a single encoding. So we can't do
something different for comments than other code.

We could eventually add UTF-8 support, but given everything else we
have to do, it's just not a high priority.

> Language lexical elements (identifiers !) are
> another matter, though... But it *is* possible.

Of course. Java lets you write Unicode in your programs. But
then you have to be careful to declare the encoding, as the default
is just by operating system and configuration.

> Exemple in R (3.0.1) :
>

> > Sélénè<-"La lune"
> > Λυσιστρατα<-"Quelle nana !"
> > ls()
> [1] "Sélénè" "Λυσιστρατα"
> |

It looks like R is using a global setting for encoding.

It's really a tricky business to get all the details right.
And as soon as you do get it right in the code, users mess it
up left and right by creating mangled docs of mixed character
encodings, forgetting to set encodings, etc.

Maybe we could go with a UTF-8 default, which is the only
thing that supports all of Unicode and is backward-compatible
with ASCII at the byte level.

- Bob

Insisting on UTF8 over other input encodings is extremely sensible. All ASCII input (and thus all current Stan code) is valid UTF8; there are large classes of errors (like endian reversal, or mistaking code points for code units) that simply can't happen in UTF8, and it's the default encoding for many tools. Also, since it's most common character encoding on the Web by far [1], it's highly likely that a text editor will support it properly. (Old versions of Notepad may be a notable exception.)

[1] http://w3techs.com/technologies/overview/character_encoding/all

From a brief skim, this might be helpful for the compiler-writers: http://www.utf8everywhere.org/

Compiling the resulting code is, unfortunately, a more complicated story, as I'm forced to conclude after lots of digging. g++ (probably 4.2+) supports the "experimental" '-fextended-identifiers' option, letting you encode your variable names with \u... or \U... [1] [2], and I tested this works with Stan-generated code. But extended identifier support only came to clang in version 3.3 [3], which is newer than /usr/bin/clang on my OS X Mountain Lion system. Promisingly, though, "/Applications/Xcode.app/Contents//Developer/Toolchains/XcodeDefault.xctoolchain/usr/bin/clang++" (from Xcode 5) is 3.3, though, and it successfully compiles my UTF-8 encoded Stan source file with no problem -- both with and without \u-encoding the characters. I don't know anything about MSVC.

[1] http://stackoverflow.com/questions/2681778/g-unicode-variable-name
[2] http://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Preprocessor-Options.html
[3] http://llvm.org/releases/3.3/tools/clang/docs/ReleaseNotes.html

Neither punycode nor percent-encoding produce valid C++ identifiers, unfortunately, though I now appreciate the sentiment behind that suggestion :) I almost suggested Base64-encoded UTF8, until I realized that it needs '.' or ':' or '+' (even though you can get away with omitting the '='s). An ugly stopgap would be: non-ASCII variable names get encoded as '_U' followed by their (4-byte) code points in hex.

Hope this helps,
-Ken

> >Insisting on UTF8 over other input encodings is extremely sensible. All ASCII input (and thus all current Stan code) is
> >valid UTF8; there are large classes of errors (like endian reversal, or mistaking code points for code units) that
> >simply can't happen in UTF8, and it's the default encoding for many tools. Also, since it's most common character
> >encoding on the Web by far [1], it's highly likely that a text editor will support it properly. (Old versions of Notepad
> >may be a notable exception.)
> >
> >[1] http://w3techs.com/technologies/overview/character_encoding/all
> >
> > From a brief skim, this might be helpful for the compiler-writers: http://www.utf8everywhere.org/
> >
> >Compiling the resulting code is, unfortunately, a more complicated story, as I'm forced to conclude after lots of
> >digging. g++ (probably 4.2+) supports the "experimental" '-fextended-identifiers' option, letting you encode your
> >variable names with \u... or \U... [1] [2], and I tested this works with Stan-generated code. But extended identifier
> >support only came to clang in version 3.3 [3], which is newer than /usr/bin/clang on my OS X Mountain Lion system.
> >Promisingly, though, "/Applications/Xcode.app/Contents//Developer/Toolchains/XcodeDefault.xctoolchain/usr/bin/clang++"
> >(from Xcode 5) is 3.3, though, and it successfully compiles my UTF-8 encoded Stan source file with no problem -- both
> >with and without \u-encoding the characters. I don't know anything about MSVC.
> >
> >[1] http://stackoverflow.com/questions/2681778/g-unicode-variable-name
> >[2] http://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Preprocessor-Options.html
> >[3] http://llvm.org/releases/3.3/tools/clang/docs/ReleaseNotes.html
> >
> >Neither punycode nor percent-encoding produce valid C++ identifiers, unfortunately, though I now appreciate the
> >sentiment behind that suggestion :) I almost suggested Base64-encoded UTF8, until I realized that it needs '.' or ':' or
> >'+' (even though you can get away with omitting the '='s). An ugly stopgap would be: non-ASCII variable names get
> >encoded as '_U' followed by their (4-byte) code points in hex.
> >
> >Hope this helps,
> >-Ken
> >
> >
> >On Sun, Oct 6, 2013 at 9:22 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>> wrote:
> >
> >
> >
> > On 10/6/13 9:06 AM, Allen Riddell wrote:
> >
> > What if UTF-8 was encoded using percent-encoding or punycode? Which would be
> > better for C++?
> >
> > - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percent_encoding#Current_standard
> > - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punycode
> >
> > I think it would be great to be able to write: 标准差 ~ cauchy(0, 2.5)
> >
> >
> > I think it'll introduce too many errors! Especially if we
> > add another layer of escaping. The problem is more in transport
> > to and from interfaces like R, Python, the shell, and text
> > editors than within a file itself.
> >
> > If we do support Unicode, then the whole doc should be in Unicode.
> > XML does this the right way. Note there's no way to declare the
> > encoding and still have the doc be in that encoding, because you
> > get a chicken and egg problem. So this means external specifications
> > of character encoding, which means things can break.
> >
> > Or we could just insist on UTF-8, which is at least ASCII compatible.
> > I don't know if it's compatible with everyone's text editors.
> >
> > - Bob

parts:
On 10/7/13 8:34 AM, Allen Riddell wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> So I take it it's not a matter of simply switching from std::string to
> std::wstring? (I know only enough C++ to injure myself.)

> PyStan could support a switch to anything (utf-8, utf-16/UCS-2) in a pinch. It
> already explicitly encodes strings to ascii when they are passed to Stan (via
> std::string).

The problem isn't whether any of these programs can easily
employ different encodings, it's about having them all talk
to each other, files, editors, and command lines where the trouble
really starts. I just want to avoid users messages like "I used
Greek characters for my variables, but it looks like %^&* in the
output."

- Bob
